sheet-33.description: Sheet 33 covers the northern part of the village of Point Pleasant, between Arnold Avenue and the Manasquan River, drawn at 120 feet to an inch with north to the right of the page. Manasquan Avenue and Curtis Avenue cross the upper half of the sheet diagonally towards the river, which curves across the upper right corner; River Avenue crosses the middle of the sheet, and Richmond Avenue and Hawthorne Avenue run across the lower part, cut by McLean Avenue, Van Note Place and Cedar Avenue. Grove Avenue and Bay Avenue meet Arnold Avenue on the left, where the outlines of sheet 37 are drawn. The tracks of the New York and Long Branch Railroad cross the lower part of the sheet, with a turntable, a railroad pump house with a water tank on its roof, and sidings marked full of tracks; south of the tracks a few lots front on River Road and on North, near the lower edge. Most of the ground north of River Avenue is in large tracts with scattered cottages, among them the Curtis House and a group of cottages in tract 92, and narrow riverside lots along the Manasquan. Along Grove and River Avenues stand the Point Pleasant Free Library and the First Baptist Church. Between Richmond and Hawthorne Avenues the blocks are cut into narrow numbered lots with frame dwellings, and beside the railroad stand an ice company with cold storage, an ice house, bottling works and an engine house, and a coal pocket. A box of notes describes the ice works' own fire protection.
notes: Drawn at 120 feet to an inch, with north to the right of the page.
Grove Avenue is Grove Street in OpenStreetMap.
The ice company is lettered Point Pleasant Regerled Ice Co., and P.P.R.I. Co. in the notes box.
The modern junction of Curtis and McLean Avenues lies about 11 m from where the sheet draws it and was not used.
Van Note Place is not in OpenStreetMap.

120 ft to an inch, north to the right. Northern Point Pleasant between Arnold Avenue and the Manasquan River: Manasquan, Curtis, River, Richmond, Hawthorne Avenues, McLean, Grove, Bay, Cedar Avenues, Van Note Place, the NY & Long Branch RR with ice works. One part. Configured by the lead.

sheet-34-1.description: Sheet 34, part 1, is the upper half of the page, above a heavy dividing line, drawn at 120 feet to an inch with north to the right of the page. It covers the western side of the old village of Point Pleasant, now the borough of Point Pleasant, along Rue Avenue and Arnold Avenue between Atlantic Avenue and the Manasquan River. Rue Avenue crosses the page from the left edge to Trenton Avenue, and Arnold Avenue continues its line east of Trenton Avenue, bending towards the river at Clark's Landing. Atlantic Avenue and Trenton Avenue run down the page to Ennis Avenue at the foot of the part, and West Avenue runs diagonally across the top left corner past Cottage Place. Between Atlantic and Trenton Avenues lies White Lawn Cemetery, filling most of block 3. The rest of the ground is divided into large, irregular lots with scattered frame dwellings, many of them lettered for the key, a few shops and stables. At Clark's Landing, on the river bank, stand a photograph gallery, a merry-go-round, an ice house, a boat builder, a gasoline engine and a large building with bath houses below, beside a water tank. East of Arnold Avenue the part reaches Manasquan Avenue and large undeveloped tracts that continue on sheet 33. The Manasquan River runs along the upper right edge of the part, and the page carries a north arrow in the upper right corner.
notes: Drawn at 120 feet to an inch, with north to the right of the page.
Ennis Avenue is Borden Avenue today (its junctions with Trenton and Atlantic Avenues match).
Modern Arnold Avenue meets Trenton Avenue about 25 m north of where the 1905 Arnold Avenue continues Rue Avenue; Arnold Avenue was left out of the control for that reason.
West Avenue and Ennis Avenue (as named) and Cottage Place and Manasquan Avenue at these positions are not in OpenStreetMap under these names.

120 ft to an inch. Two parts divided by a heavy horizontal line: part 1 (upper half, north to the right) Rue, Arnold, Trenton, Atlantic and Ennis (now Borden) Avenues, White Lawn Cemetery and Clark's Landing in the borough of Point Pleasant; part 2 (lower half, north to the upper left) River, Curtis and Cedar Avenues by the Manasquan River and the bridge to Brielle. Configured by the lead.

sheet-34-2.description: Sheet 34, part 2, is the lower half of the page, below a heavy dividing line, drawn at 120 feet to an inch with north towards the upper left. It shows the north end of the village of Point Pleasant on the south bank of the Manasquan River, between Curtis Avenue and the tracks of the New York and Long Branch Railroad. River Avenue runs down the page from the Bridge to Brielle on the river bank to Cedar Avenue at the foot, where Richmond Avenue branches off to the southeast; Curtis Avenue runs parallel to it on the west, and North Avenue crosses the railroad near the lower right corner. The ground is laid out in a few large tracts, numbered 117 and 118 on the key, with only scattered buildings: frame dwellings and stables along Curtis and River Avenues, a windmill, and a house near the bridge approach. The Manasquan River curves across the left and upper part of the page, with its name lettered along the water, and the railroad runs on its own right of way from the river down to the bottom edge, past the start of North Avenue. The rest of the part is blank paper with the edges of sheet 33 indicated.
notes: Drawn at 120 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper left.
The road lettered Bridge to Brielle leads to the bridge over the Manasquan River at the head of River Avenue.
Placed from two points only (Cedar Avenue at Curtis Avenue, and the hand-picked fork of River and Richmond Avenues at Cedar Avenue): helmert, low confidence away from Cedar Avenue.

120 ft to an inch. Two parts divided by a heavy horizontal line: part 1 (upper half, north to the right) Rue, Arnold, Trenton, Atlantic and Ennis (now Borden) Avenues, White Lawn Cemetery and Clark's Landing in the borough of Point Pleasant; part 2 (lower half, north to the upper left) River, Curtis and Cedar Avenues by the Manasquan River and the bridge to Brielle. Configured by the lead.

sheet-35.description: Sheet 35 covers the western business and residential district of Point Pleasant in 1905, today on the boundary of the boroughs of Point Pleasant and Point Pleasant Beach. It is drawn at 120 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page and reaches from Arnold Avenue along the top edge south to Newark Avenue, and from Ennis Avenue in the west to Richmond Avenue in the east. Trenton, Forman, Atlantic and New Jersey Avenues cross the sheet from west to east; Howard Avenue, Gowdy Avenue and Bay Avenue run south from Trenton Avenue, Gowdy and Bay Avenues continuing as long diagonal roads to the lower edge, with lots numbered along both sides. Laurel Avenue enters from the east at the top right. The blocks between Trenton and New Jersey Avenues are divided into narrow numbered lots, many with frame dwellings. Institutions here include the public school and the First Presbyterian Church between Trenton and Forman Avenues, St. Mary's by the Sea between Forman and Atlantic Avenues, St. Vincent's Home and the Warwick Arms on Richmond Avenue. North of Trenton Avenue, in block 91, are the Hotel Marion, R. Van Note's livery stable with a windmill, a bottling works, a pool room, a carpenter shop and offices. The southern half of the sheet is mostly undeveloped land in large tracts (35 to 37), with a few scattered buildings near Gowdy Avenue and the lower edge. Along Richmond Avenue the edges of sheets 41 and 43 are drawn, with the short ends of New York, Philadelphia, Washington and Newark Avenues.
notes: Drawn at 120 feet to an inch.
Ennis Avenue is Borden Avenue today.
Bay Avenue is also lettered (Squan) where it leaves the town to the south.
New York, Philadelphia and Washington Avenues are lettered in abbreviated form (N.Y., Phila., Wash.).

120 ft to an inch, north up. Western district: Trenton, Forman, Atlantic, New Jersey Avenues between Ennis (Borden) and Richmond Avenues, Howard, Gowdy and Bay (Squan) Avenues south to the town edge. One part. Configured by the lead.

sheet-37.description: Sheet 37 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas covers the western edge of the built-up village, now the centre of Point Pleasant Beach and the adjoining part of Point Pleasant borough. It lies between Bay Avenue and the angled line of River Avenue on the west and Richmond Avenue on the east, from McLean Avenue at the top to Trenton Avenue at the foot, with Grove, Arnold and Laurel Avenues crossing it. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page and a compass rose in the upper left; the numbered neighbouring sheets are 33 and 35 on the west and 38 and 41 on the east and south. The railroad runs down the right-hand margin. The densest building is along Bay Avenue and the blocks on either side of Arnold Avenue, where the sheet shows a bakery and bake house, grocery and dry goods stores, a post office, a borough hall with fire house, opera house and lodge room, Central House and a department store, all in frame or brick buildings of one to three storeys. Along River Avenue a row of lettered lots carries large frame dwellings with outbuildings, and the Maple Grove Hotel, with its kitchen, water tank and gasoline engine, stands near the middle of the sheet. East of it the Hotel Richmond and its livery stand at Richmond Avenue. The blocks between Arnold and Trenton Avenues are laid out in narrow numbered lots and mostly empty, with scattered dwellings, a green-tinted building on Richmond Avenue lettered as a paint and furniture store. Street widths are lettered as 50, 60 and 65 feet.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
The bearing of River Avenue is angled to the street grid; the sheet is slightly skewed along the Bay Avenue side.
Grove Avenue is Grove Street in OpenStreetMap and River Avenue is River Road there.
60 ft to an inch. Grove, Arnold, Laurel and Trenton Avenues between Richmond, McLean and Bay Avenues. Bay Avenue points carry about 3 m. One part.

sheet-38.description: Sheet 38 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas shows the area east of the railroad in the north of the village, now Point Pleasant Beach. The New York and Long Branch Railroad, drawn as a wide fan of parallel tracks, runs down the left edge, with the stone depot, an express and baggage room, a freight house, an ice house and a small storage building on its east side. East of the tracks the sheet is a grid of blocks bounded by Central, Arnold, Laurel and Trenton Avenues running across, and by St. Louis Avenue and Chicago Avenue running down, with River Road cutting in diagonally at the top. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page and a compass rose at the left margin. Most of the blocks are laid out in narrow numbered lots (blocks 106, 107, 95, 96, 88, 87, 78 and 79) and are almost entirely vacant. The few buildings stand in the north-western corner: Downey's coal yard with its coal pockets beside River Road, a lumber yard and shingle store of Van Note and Son on the edge of block 95, a sash shop and a few dwellings. Street widths are lettered as 60 feet. The right-hand margin carries the numbers of the adjoining sheets 39, 42, 41 and 37, and the sheet number 38 and the legend title in the top corner.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
The railroad is lettered New York and Long Branch R.R.; today it is the North Jersey Coast Line.
St. Louis Avenue is Saint Louis Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Laurel Avenue near St. Louis Avenue is Laurel Court there.
60 ft to an inch. Central, Arnold, Laurel and Trenton Avenues between the railroad and Chicago Avenue, St. Louis Avenue. One part.

sheet-39.description: Sheet 39 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas shows the northern blocks of the village, now part of Point Pleasant Beach, west of Little Silver Lake. Central, Arnold, Laurel and Trenton Avenues cross the sheet from west to east, and Chicago Avenue, Baltimore Avenue and Boston Avenue run down it, with the unlettered northern edge of the sheet cut by an angled boundary line at the top. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page, a compass rose standing in the open lakeside ground at the right, and the scale bar at the foot. Nearly all of the blocks are drawn as grids of narrow numbered lots (blocks 108, 101, 97, 98, 86, 85 and 80) and are vacant, the street edges and lot lines being all that is printed; the only buildings are a few frame dwellings with outbuildings, three in the blocks north and south of Central Avenue near Boston Avenue and one nearer the middle of the sheet. Little Silver Lake, shown with a light blue tint, fills the lower right quarter, its inlet curving up between Baltimore and Boston Avenues to the line of Arnold Avenue and narrowing at the foot of the sheet where it passes under Trenton Avenue. Block 85 beside the lake is cut by its irregular shore. Street widths are lettered as 60 feet. The adjoining sheets named in the margins are 38, 40, 42 and 45.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
Laurel Avenue near Baltimore and Chicago Avenues is Laurel Court in OpenStreetMap, and the Laurel / Baltimore junction shares a node with Trenton Avenue there.
60 ft to an inch. Central, Arnold, Laurel and Trenton Avenues, Chicago, Baltimore and Boston Avenues, Little Silver Lake. One part.

sheet-40.description: Sheet 40 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas reaches the ocean front of what is now Point Pleasant Beach, east of Little Silver Lake. Boston Avenue runs down the left edge, Central and Arnold Avenues cross from it towards the shore and Trenton Avenue closes the foot of the sheet. Ocean Avenue runs along the beach as two angled strips, one in the upper right, where it is lettered Ocean Avenue between blocks 100 and 99 and the shore, and one in the lower middle between blocks 84 and 83. The sheet is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top and a compass rose in the open ground beside the lake. Block 100 at the top and blocks 99, 82, 84 and 83 are laid out in lots, mostly vacant. Block 99 near Ocean Avenue holds a cluster of long, narrow frame buildings set at an angle to the streets, with a larger two-storey building with open first floor at its southern end; two large frame dwellings stand on the ocean side of block 83, and a few small houses stand in the north-west and south-west blocks. A dashed double line lettered Board Walk, with yellow cross strokes, runs along the foot of the beach lots. The Atlantic Ocean fills the right edge, with the surf line tinted blue. Little Silver Lake occupies the open ground at the left between Arnold and Trenton Avenues, drawn with a pale blue inlet and a heavy line at its north shore. Street widths are lettered 50, 60 and 70 feet.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.

Ocean Avenue is drawn in two pieces: south of Arnold Avenue it matches modern Ocean Avenue (its junctions with Arnold and Trenton Avenues are used), but the stretch drawn north of Arnold Avenue, offset about 100 m east, does not match modern Ocean Avenue at Central Avenue and was not used.
The boardwalk is lettered Board Walk.

60 ft to an inch. Central and Arnold Avenues to the beach, Boston Avenue, Little Silver Lake. Ocean Avenue drawn in two pieces: the stretch south of Arnold matches modern Ocean Avenue; the stretch north of Arnold, offset about 100 m east, does not (Central/Ocean excluded). One part.

sheet-41.description: Sheet 41 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas covers four blocks of the centre of what is now Point Pleasant Beach, between Richmond Avenue on the west and St. Louis Avenue on the east, from Trenton Avenue in the north to New York Avenue in the south, with Forman, Atlantic and New Jersey Avenues crossing between them. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page. The tracks of the Pennsylvania Railroad run north to south down the middle of the sheet, splitting each block into a western half (blocks 71, 59, 52 and 39) and an eastern half (Pleasure Park and blocks 60, 51 and 40). The blocks are laid out in narrow numbered lots, most of them still empty; scattered frame dwellings stand on them, with a drug store at the corner of Richmond and Trenton Avenues. The northern half of the block between Trenton and Forman Avenues east of the railroad is the open ground of Pleasure Park. St. Peter's Roman Catholic Church and its rectory stand at the corner of Forman and St. Louis Avenues. On the east side of the railroad between Atlantic and New Jersey Avenues are the works of the Point Pleasant Electric Light and Power Company, a fireproof engine house with dynamos, engines and a brick boiler house, beside a coal bin and a spur track, together with a car barn and repair shop and the Point Pleasant Water Works with its water tank. Several cottages carry names, among them Averne and Ardmore. The margins show the edges of the adjoining sheets 35, 37, 38, 42 and 43, and the scale bar is printed at the foot.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
The railroad is lettered Pennsylvania R.R.; today it is the North Jersey Coast Line.
St. Louis Avenue is Saint Louis Avenue in OpenStreetMap.

60 ft to an inch, north up. Pilot sheet. Trenton, Forman, Atlantic, New Jersey and New York Avenues between Richmond and St. Louis Avenues, Pennsylvania RR down the middle, Pleasure Park, electric light works. One part.

sheet-42.description: Sheet 42 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas covers a regular grid of blocks in the middle of the village, now Point Pleasant Beach, between St. Louis Avenue on the west and Baltimore Avenue on the east, with Chicago Avenue dividing it down the middle. Trenton, Forman, Atlantic, New Jersey and New York Avenues cross it from north to south. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page, a compass rose standing beside Little Silver Lake, and the scale bar at the foot. Blocks 70, 61, 50, 41, 69, 62, 49 and 42 are cut into narrow numbered lots, and most are empty. Buildings are few and cluster in the western half: a row of frame dwellings along St. Louis Avenue, the three-storey frame Point Pleasant Cottage with its annexes on the north side of Atlantic Avenue, and The Gladstone, a large three-storey frame hotel, with a neighbouring two-and-a-half storey dwelling on the south side of the avenue. Two more dwellings stand at the Baltimore Avenue side and a cluster of small cottages near Forman Avenue. The upper right corner is taken by Little Silver Lake, drawn with a blue-tinted shore band, with its inlet running off the right edge. Street widths are lettered as 50 and 60 feet. The adjoining sheets named in the margins are 38, 39, 41, 44 and 45.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
St. Louis Avenue is Saint Louis Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
60 ft to an inch. Trenton to New York Avenues between St. Louis and Baltimore Avenues, Chicago Avenue, Little Silver Lake. One part.

sheet-43.description: Sheet 43 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas covers the blocks on both sides of the railroad in the south-west of what is now Point Pleasant Beach. Richmond Avenue bounds it on the west and St. Louis Avenue on the east, and New York, Philadelphia, Washington, Newark and Lake Avenues cross from top to bottom. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page; a compass rose stands in the open ground beside St. Louis Avenue. The double track of the Penn. R.R. runs down the middle of the sheet, and splits each block into a western and an eastern half. The blocks (34, 33, 23, 24, 22, 21, 16 and 15 around the railroad, and 14 at the foot) are laid out in narrow numbered lots in two rows, with no buildings at all on the sheet. A diagonal line crosses the lower left and then the lower right of the sheet, cutting the corners of the lots at Newark Avenue and Lake Avenue; it is a property boundary at an angle to the grid, and beyond it the sheet is blank. On the right edge a blue-tinted strip of water, unlabelled on this sheet, runs down the east side of St. Louis Avenue and bends along the foot. Street widths are lettered 50 and 60 feet. The adjoining sheets named in the margins are 35, 36 and 44.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
The railroad is lettered Penn. R.R.; today it is the North Jersey Coast Line.
St. Louis Avenue is Saint Louis Avenue in OpenStreetMap. Lake Avenue has no junction with the other listed streets in OpenStreetMap and was not used for control.
Newark Avenue does not meet Richmond Avenue in OpenStreetMap, so that corner was not used for control.
60 ft to an inch. New York, Philadelphia, Washington, Newark and Lake Avenues between Richmond and St. Louis Avenues. One part.

sheet-44-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 44 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas is the main map of the sheet: eight blocks of the grid between New York Avenue at the top and Newark Avenue near the foot, bounded by St. Louis Avenue on the west and Baltimore Avenue on the east, with Chicago Avenue dividing the blocks in two columns. Philadelphia and Washington Avenues cross between them. It lies in the southern part of today's Point Pleasant Beach and is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page. The blocks (32, 31, 25, 26, 20 and 19) are laid out in narrow numbered lots, in two rows of about twenty lots each, and none carries a building: the part is an unbuilt residential tract. Along the south side the map turns to water. A blue-tinted channel with a heavy double line runs along Newark Avenue to the west, bends north around the corner of block 19 and then east to the right edge, enclosing the area south of the blocks, while Mineral Lake extends as a narrow strip down the left margin below Newark Avenue, with a compass rose beside it. The part is cut at its lower right by a heavy line enclosing an inset of the Pine Bluff Inn and Cottage Company on the Manasquan River, which is a separate part and not covered here. Street widths are lettered as 60 feet. The adjoining sheets named in the margins are 42, 43, 46 and 45.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
St. Louis Avenue is Saint Louis Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The mask leaves out the inset of the Pine Bluff Inn and Cottage Company at the lower right (part 2, not placed).

60 ft to an inch. Part 1: New York to Newark Avenues between St. Louis and Baltimore Avenues, Chicago Avenue, Mineral Lake. Part 2 (lower right, inside a heavy line, own north arrow): inset of the Pine Bluff Inn and Cottage Co. on the Manasquan River, on Pine Bluff Inn Av, "located 3/4 mile W.N.W. of P.O."; not placed.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Pine Bluff Inn and Cottage Co. on the Manasquan River (Pine Bluff Inn Av) (one street and no junction; the inset's location (3/4 mile W.N.W. of the post office) does not match modern Pine Bluff Avenue clearly; needs hand-picked control from parcel corners or the river shore).

sheet-45.description: Sheet 45 of the 1905 Point Pleasant atlas shows the beach-front blocks of what is now Point Pleasant Beach, from Little Silver Lake in the north-east corner to the Atlantic Ocean along the bottom. The sheet is drawn turned about a quarter turn from the neighbouring ones, so that north points to the right: Baltimore Avenue runs along the top, Boston Avenue across the middle, and New York, New Jersey, Atlantic, Forman and Trenton Avenues run down the page from left to right. Ocean Avenue crosses the lower part at a slant, following the shore, with the Board Walk, a dashed double line with yellow cross strokes, just beyond it. The sheet is drawn at 60 feet to an inch. North of Boston Avenue the blocks (43, 48, 63 and 68) are laid out in numbered lots with a scatter of frame dwellings; Land's End Hotel stands on the New Jersey Avenue corner and The Carrollton, a large frame hotel, at Atlantic Avenue. South of Boston Avenue, blocks 44, 45, 47, 64 and 67 carry more dwellings. Block 46 on the Ocean Avenue front holds the bathing complex: a grid of narrow bath houses, a Pavilion and an Amusement Hall opening on the Board Walk. Further east, blocks 65 and 66 hold a few cottages and The Leighton, a large three-and-a-half storey hotel with wings and a circular porch at the lower right. The ocean, tinted blue with a heavy shore line, occupies the lower left corner and bottom edge, with a compass rose on the beach. Street widths are lettered as 60 and 70 feet.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
The sheet is turned: its rotation is about 96 degrees rather than the 6 degrees of its neighbours.
Ocean Avenue as drawn does not follow OpenStreetMap's Ocean Avenue, so it was not used for control.
The boardwalk is lettered Board Walk.
60 ft to an inch, turned about 96 degrees (north to the right). Baltimore and Boston Avenues from Trenton to New Jersey and New York Avenues, Ocean Avenue along the shore (left out). One part.

sheet-46-1.description: Sheet 46, part 1, covers the southeastern corner of the 1905 town plan of what is now Point Pleasant Beach, between Baltimore Avenue on the west and the Atlantic Ocean on the east, from New York Avenue in the north past Philadelphia and Washington Avenues to the north end of Mineral Lake. It is drawn at 60 feet to an inch with north at the top of the page. Ocean Avenue crosses the sheet diagonally from north-northeast to south-southwest, and a boardwalk runs along the beach east of it, close to the line of the surf. The blocks between Baltimore and Ocean Avenues (30, 27 and 18) and the shallower blocks between Ocean Avenue and the beach (29 and 28) are cut into narrow numbered lots, almost all of them still empty. Only a handful of frame dwellings stand on them: the Berean Retreat and two cottages on New York Avenue, a house on Philadelphia Avenue, a house marked as being built at Washington Avenue, and a few small buildings and a long row of bath houses on the beach block between Philadelphia and Washington Avenues. South of Washington Avenue the long block 17 runs down the east side of Ocean Avenue beside the open water of Mineral Lake, which is drawn along the western margin and again in the narrow strip beside a heavy dividing line. A heavy line separates this part from part 2 in the lower right corner of the page, which continues Baltimore and Ocean Avenues to the south. The edges of the adjoining sheets 44 and 45 are drawn in the margins, and the scale bar is at the foot.
notes: Drawn at 60 feet to an inch.
Lots 38 to 40 of block 17 are repeated at the top of part 2; part 2 is placed from them.

60 ft to an inch. Part 1: New York, Philadelphia and Washington Avenues between Baltimore Avenue and the beach, Ocean Avenue, block 17 down to Mineral Lake. Part 2 (lower right, inside a heavy line): Baltimore and Ocean Avenues continued south, no cross street; placed from lot corners repeated on part 1. Configured by the lead.

sheet-46-2.description: Sheet 46, part 2, is the lower right corner of the page, set off from part 1 by a heavy line. It continues Baltimore Avenue and Ocean Avenue southward along the beach of what is now Point Pleasant Beach, south of the point where part 1 stops, and is drawn at the same 60 feet to an inch and with the same orientation, north at the top. Mineral Lake is drawn as a narrow strip of water between the dividing line and the west side of Baltimore Avenue. Between Baltimore and Ocean Avenues lies a narrow wedge of block 18 with lots 16 to 18; east of Ocean Avenue the long block 17 is divided into two rows of deep lots, numbered 39 to 51 along Ocean Avenue and 14 to 1 towards the beach, and the Atlantic Ocean is drawn along the east edge of the page. No buildings stand on any of these lots in 1905. The first rows of lots, 38 to 40 and 15 to 13, repeat lots already drawn at the foot of part 1, and lines at the bottom of the part mark the southern edge of the platted ground. No cross street is drawn, so the part was placed by carrying two lot corners from part 1 and holding its scale and rotation to part 1's; its position along the beach is only as good as that transfer.
